description:
We are ASTHRAL, a team passionate about biomedical engineering, AI, medicine, and space exploration. We're developing an offline-first health monitoring and medical decision-support system to help astronauts assess risks and access evidence-based guidance during long-duration missions.

We welcome teammates skilled in aerospace engineering, medicine, machine learning, software development, and UI/UX design. Join us in shaping the future of astronaut healthcare!
summary:
ASTHRAL is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring and medical decision-support research prototype designed for long-duration space missions, where communication delays and limited access to medical professionals can make timely health assessment challenging.

Our platform brings together physiological monitoring, longitudinal health records, deterministic biomedical assessment, and an optional local AI assistant. It allows astronauts to review health indicators, identify changes over time, explore potential health concerns, and receive traceable decision-support information without depending on continuous Internet connectivity.

The system incorporates evidence-informed clinical pathways, personal health histories, and research modules for mission-related risks, including extravehicular activity and space radiation. NASA medical standards, human spaceflight research, and public radiation resources inform its development.

By combining biomedical engineering, explainable software, and offline capabilities, ASTHRAL aims to increase crew autonomy while maintaining clear boundaries between supporting medical decisions and making clinical diagnoses. The current implementation is a research prototype evaluated primarily with synthetic scenarios, with clinical and operational validation remaining future objectives.
details:
GitHub Code Link:

https://github.com/GiaDiGr/ASTHRAL

What exactly does ASTHRAL do?

ASTHRAL provides an integrated environment for astronaut health monitoring and decision support. It is designed to help crew members assess their health during long-duration missions, particularly when immediate medical guidance from Earth may be unavailable.

The platform supports the collection and organization of physiological measurements and health observations, longitudinal visualization, rule-based clinical assessment, and access to supporting biomedical information.

Its biomedical research engine currently implements seven clinical assessment pathways, including diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, hypoglycemia, orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, acute kidney injury, and anaphylaxis.

Additional research components explore computer vision, voice-based health reporting, mission monitoring, radiation data visualization, and simulated extravehicular activities.

How does it work?

ASTHRAL follows a structured workflow that combines input validation, data processing, evidence-based rules, and user interaction.

First, physiological measurements and health observations are obtained from manually entered information or synthetic mission scenarios. These inputs are checked for completeness, units, and validity before further processing.

The system then organizes measurements into longitudinal health records and evaluates applicable clinical criteria using a deterministic biomedical engine. This approach makes it possible to trace why particular findings were generated while identifying missing measurements or information that requires professional review.

A browser-based dashboard presents health information and allows users to explore their history and assessment results.

ASTHRAL is designed to operate offline using locally available software, stored data, and scientific references. Its optional local AI assistant supports information retrieval and explanation, while clinical findings remain governed by the deterministic engine rather than the language model.

Research modules also incorporate public NASA environmental and radiation resources. Historical radiation measurements and space-weather information are kept separate from personal medical measurements and simulated mission data.

What benefits does it have?

Greater autonomy: Astronauts can access health information and decision-support functionality even when communication with Earth is interrupted.

Explainability: Deterministic rules and traceable sources make findings more transparent than relying exclusively on AI-generated responses.

Longitudinal monitoring: Organized health histories allow users to examine changes and potential trends over time.

Offline functionality: Local operation reduces dependence on external servers and continuous connectivity.

Modular design: The architecture supports the future integration of additional medical pathways, monitoring devices, and research modules.

Safety-oriented design: The system distinguishes measured information, simulated data, missing evidence, and unvalidated conclusions.

What do we hope to achieve?

Our long-term objective is to develop ASTHRAL into a scientifically evaluated health-support platform suitable for increasingly autonomous space missions.

Future work includes integrating validated physiological sensors, expanding spaceflight-specific monitoring, strengthening privacy and security, evaluating usability with representative users, and conducting independent clinical and operational validation.

Beyond space exploration, the underlying architecture could also be useful for remote healthcare settings on Earth, where reliable communication and specialized medical support are limited.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

ASTHRAL's software architecture uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, JavaScript, and browser-based technologies.

The biomedical assessment engine is developed in Python, while the interface supports interactive visualization, offline storage, and access to structured findings.

Optional AI components include a locally deployed Qwen3 language model through Ollama, local information retrieval, and experimental speech recognition using Vosk. Research-oriented visualization components include Three.js and orbital propagation utilities.

GitHub is used for source-code management and technical documentation, while Cloudflare Pages supports the browser-based demonstration.

The current project is principally a software prototype. Physiological sensor hardware integration remains a future development objective rather than a validated component of the current system.
